ecdc_inv.title: ECDC: Guidelines for the surveillance of invasive mosquitoes in Europe

ecdc_nat.title: ECDC: Guidelines for the surveillance of native mosquitoes in Europe

content.summary: An invasive, day-biting mosquito that breeds in small containers of water. Established across much of southern and central Europe and detected in the UK on several occasions, usually near ports, motorway services and freight routes. A priority species for surveillance.
identification: Black body with bright white scales
A single white stripe running down the middle of the thorax (top of the body behind the head)
White bands on the legs
Small: around 2 to 10 mm
breeding_habitats: Small water-holding containers: tyres, plant-pot saucers, buckets, water butts, blocked gutters, tarpaulins
Tree holes and other natural containers
Eggs are laid just above the waterline and survive drying out for months
content.activity: Bites mainly during the day, with peaks in the early morning and late afternoon; aggressive and persistent biter, often outdoors.
content.season: In Europe mainly active from late spring to autumn; eggs can overwinter.
content.uk_status: Not established in the UK. Detections are reported to and coordinated with UKHSA. Treat any finding as a possible incursion.
diseases: Can transmit dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses (local transmission has occurred in Europe)
lures: BG-Lure or similar human-skin odour lure with BG-Sentinel; CO2 increases catches

content.summary: An invasive, container-breeding mosquito of tropical and subtropical regions, closely associated with people and buildings. Not established in the UK; occasional introductions are possible through ports and airports.
identification: Dark body with white scales
A lyre-shaped pattern of white scales on the thorax
White bands on the legs
breeding_habitats: Artificial containers in and around buildings: water storage, flower vases, tyres, discarded containers
content.activity: Bites during the day, often indoors or close to houses.
content.season: Needs warm conditions; unlikely to survive UK winters outdoors.
content.uk_status: Not established in the UK. Any detection is significant and should be reported to UKHSA.
diseases: The main vector of dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya and Zika viruses worldwide

content.summary: An invasive container-breeding mosquito, established in parts of central and western Europe. Tolerates cooler climates than Aedes albopictus.
identification: Dark body with golden-yellow stripes (lines) on the thorax
White bands on the legs
breeding_habitats: Rock pools, tree holes and artificial containers such as tyres, water butts and cemetery vases
content.season: Active from spring to autumn; tolerates cool temperatures.
content.uk_status: Detections have been reported in the UK; check the current position with UKHSA.
diseases: A potential vector of several viruses in laboratory studies; its role in transmission in Europe is considered limited

content.summary: A native coastal mosquito that breeds in brackish water in salt marshes. Can be a significant nuisance biter in coastal communities.
identification: Brown mosquito with pale bands on the legs; identification to species normally needs a microscope and key
breeding_habitats: Brackish water in coastal salt marshes and grazing marshes
content.activity: Bites readily, including during the day near breeding sites.
content.season: Can be active from early spring to late autumn.
content.uk_status: Native and widespread in suitable coastal habitats.
diseases: Mainly a nuisance species; considered a potential vector in some studies

content.summary: A native floodwater mosquito that can emerge in large numbers after flooding of river meadows and grassland.
identification: Brown mosquito with narrow pale bands on the leg joints
breeding_habitats: Temporary flood pools on river floodplains and wet grassland
content.activity: Mainly bites at dusk and night; can disperse several kilometres.
content.uk_status: Native; found in parts of the UK.
diseases: A potential vector of some viruses; mainly a nuisance species in the UK

content.summary: A native tree-hole mosquito that has adapted to breed in artificial habitats such as tyres and water-filled containers rich in organic matter.
identification: Dark grey-blue mosquito; rests with its body at an angle to the surface (typical of Anopheles)
breeding_habitats: Tyres and containers with decaying leaves and organic matter
content.activity: Bites people readily, often at dusk and during the day in shade.
diseases: Capable of transmitting malaria parasites in laboratory conditions; considered a low risk in the UK

content.summary: A group of closely related Anopheles species (a species complex). Some members historically transmitted malaria in Europe, including the UK.
identification: Dark spots on the wings
Rests at an angle to the surface
Species within the complex can only be told apart reliably by egg features or molecular methods
breeding_habitats: Large, clean, still or slow-moving water with vegetation: ditches, ponds, marsh edges; some species tolerate brackish water
content.activity: Mainly dusk and night; some members enter buildings and animal housing.
content.season: Adults overwinter in sheltered places such as outbuildings.
content.uk_status: Native members of the complex are present in the UK.
diseases: Historical vectors of malaria in Europe

content.summary: The common house mosquito: one of the most widespread mosquitoes in the UK, including in towns. Forms with different behaviour exist within the group.
identification: Light brown mosquito with pale bands on the abdomen
No pattern of white scales on the legs
breeding_habitats: Water butts, drains, ponds, ditches, blocked gutters and other standing water, often rich in organic matter
content.activity: Mostly dusk and night; one form commonly bites people and enters buildings.
content.season: Spring to autumn; females overwinter in buildings and cellars.
diseases: The main vector of West Nile virus in Europe (not currently circulating in the UK); also Usutu virus, detected in UK birds

content.summary: A wetland mosquito of reed beds and marshes, recorded in parts of south-east England.
identification: Small brown Culex; identification needs a microscope and key
breeding_habitats: Reed beds, ditches and marshland with emergent vegetation
content.activity: Bites birds and people, mainly at dusk and night.
content.uk_status: Present locally in parts of England.
diseases: A potential bridge vector of West Nile virus between birds and people

content.summary: A large, common mosquito often found around homes and gardens; frequently noticed because of its size.
identification: Large mosquito with dark spots on the wings
Clear pale bands on the legs
breeding_habitats: Water butts, ditches, ponds and other standing water, including polluted water
content.activity: Mainly dusk and night; females often enter buildings in autumn.
content.season: Adults can be seen in most months; females overwinter in buildings.
diseases: Mainly a nuisance species in the UK

content.summary: Use this when a mosquito has not been, or cannot be, identified to species: for example damaged specimens, or before the laboratory has reported. Record it as pending or inconclusive rather than guessing.
identification: Long thin legs, a long proboscis (mouthparts) and scales on the wing veins distinguish mosquitoes from other small flies
content.notes: Send unidentified specimens for identification where they may be invasive species.

content.summary: A collapsible fabric trap that draws mosquitoes in with an upward airflow and a lure that mimics human skin odour. The standard adult trap for container-breeding Aedes.
content.how_it_works: A fan pulls air into a central funnel; attracted mosquitoes are drawn into a catch bag. A skin-odour lure (and optionally CO2) increases catches.
setup: Place on the ground on a level surface
Fit the lure and, if used, the CO2 supply
Check the fan runs and the catch bag is secure
placement: In shade, sheltered from wind and rain
Near likely resting or breeding sites (vegetation, containers)
Away from competing attractants such as lights
content.servicing: Collect the catch bag at least every 24 to 72 hours, depending on the programme, and replace the lure as the manufacturer advises.
tips: Record the exact run time: it is the collection effort
Label the catch bag with trap, site and date before removing it
common_mistakes: Running out of power without noticing (record as not completed, not no catch)
Placing in full sun or exposed wind

content.summary: A small dark container with water and a surface for egg-laying (a paddle or strip). Simple and cheap; the standard early-warning trap for container-breeding Aedes.
content.how_it_works: Gravid females lay eggs on the paddle just above the waterline. Paddles are collected and eggs counted and identified.
setup: Fill with water (some programmes add a hay infusion)
Fit a fresh paddle or strip
placement: On or near the ground, sheltered
Near likely breeding habitat such as tyres or containers
content.servicing: Replace paddles and water usually every 1 to 2 weeks; never leave longer than about 7 days in warm weather, so it can't become a breeding site.
tips: Many traps across an area give a better picture than a few
Keep paddles dry and labelled for the laboratory
common_mistakes: Leaving it unserviced so larvae hatch and adults emerge
Letting it dry out (no water: record as not completed)

image.caption: An ovitrap

content.summary: A portable battery trap with a small light and fan, often baited with CO2 (dry ice or gas). Widely used for night-active species.
content.how_it_works: Light and CO2 attract host-seeking mosquitoes; a fan draws them into a collection net or container.
setup: Hang about 1.5 m above the ground
Fit charged battery and CO2 source
placement: Sheltered spot near vegetation or wetland edges
content.servicing: Collect the catch each morning and keep it cool for identification.
tips: Record start and end times for collection effort
common_mistakes: Flat battery overnight (record as not completed)
Catch left in the sun, damaging specimens

content.summary: A trap that attracts egg-laying (gravid) females with a tray of organically enriched water. Good for Culex and for virus testing because caught females have usually already fed.
content.how_it_works: Females approaching the water to lay eggs are drawn up by a fan into a collection chamber.
setup: Fill the tray with an infusion (e.g. hay or grass water) prepared in advance
Fit the fan unit and collection chamber
placement: On the ground in shade, near drains, gardens or standing water
content.servicing: Collect daily; replace the infusion regularly.
tips: Keep infusion recipe and age consistent so results are comparable
common_mistakes: Infusion too fresh or too old, reducing catches

image.file: File:CDC Gravid Trap for Mosquito Surveillance and Captured Culex Mosquito.jpg
image.caption: A gravid trap

content.summary: A commercial trap that produces CO2 and warmth (often from propane) to attract biting mosquitoes. Sometimes used for longer-term catches.
content.how_it_works: CO2, heat and moisture (and optionally a lure) attract mosquitoes, which are drawn into a net by a fan.
setup: Follow the manufacturer's instructions for the gas supply and lure
placement: Upwind of breeding areas, in shade, away from people
content.servicing: Empty the net regularly; check the gas supply.
tips: Note the gas and lure used: they affect what is caught
common_mistakes: Running out of gas without noticing

content.summary: Sampling larvae and pupae from standing water with a standard dipper. Finds breeding sites directly and supports control decisions.
content.how_it_works: A dipper (typically about 350 ml) is lowered into the water at an angle; larvae and pupae are counted and collected for identification.
setup: Use a standard dipper and a white tray
Approach the water gently so larvae don't dive
placement: Edges of standing water, among vegetation
Containers such as tyres and water butts (use a pipette for small containers)
content.servicing: Record the number of dips per site so results are comparable.
tips: Record water type (fresh, brackish), shade and vegetation
common_mistakes: Too few dips to detect low numbers
